title: Analysis and Risk Mitigations for Loss of EMS Functions 2018-2020

sentences.text: The document includes identification and a discussion of reliability and security risks due to the loss of EMS functions and presents risk mitigation strategies used by industry.

Therefore, the NERC EMSWG conducted an assessment and published NERC Energy Management System Performance Special Assessment (2018–2019)4 as an interim activity between recurring updates to its EMS reference document by using 2018–2019 EMS events reported through the ERO EAP.

To gain a better resolution on the contribution of EMS outages to the loss of situational awareness risk and the effect of EOP-004-4, the ERO Event Analysis Program identified a need to continue the analysis by adding 2020 EMS events reported through the ERO EAP into the study period.

This document includes analysis for three factors (outage duration, EMS functions, and entity reliability functions), examining associated trends, event root causes, and contributing causes identified through the ERO Cause Code Assignment Process (CCAP) for the 2018–2020 period.
From 2018–2020, the loss of EMS functions did not lead to the loss of generation, transmission lines, or customer load.
The number of reported EMS events declined from 88 in 2018, to 74 in 2019, and 58 in 2020.
The overall median outage duration remained steady, 60 minutes in 2018 and 2019, and 62.5 minutes in 2020.  EOP-004-4 is affecting EMS event reporting.
The number of state estimator/real time contingency analysis (SE/RTCA) and inter-control center protocol (ICCP) losses have declined between 2018 and 2020.
Comparing to the 2018 data, the number of loss of SE/RTCA significantly declined by 25% in 2019 and 60% in 2020, respectively.
It appears entities are now interpreting that partial loss events (such as loss of SE/RTCA, loss of ICCP) no longer require reporting.

This change in interpretation will likely reduce the data available for trending through the voluntary ERO EAP and ERO CCAP.  Entities minimized the operational degradation from the loss of situational awareness risk due to EMS outage.
The median outage duration of the TO/TOP EMS events was 60 minutes in all three years.
Generation Owners (GOs)/Generation Operators (GOPs) reported two EMS events in 2020.
Both GO/GOP events were loss of remote terminal unit (RTU).  Loss of SCADA became the most prevalent EMS failure in 2020.
Due to a significant decline of loss of SE/RTCA events, loss of SCADA became the most prevalent EMS failure in 2020, encompassing approximately 52% of all 58 EMS events reported in 2020.
It was notable that the number of loss of SCADA events increased from 24 in 2019 to 30 in 2020.

But over the evaluation period from 2018– 2020, the loss of SE/RTCA is still the most prevalent EMS failure with 103 events or 47% of all EMS events reported from 2018–2020.  The Management/Organization5 cause coding category was identified as the leading root cause.
Management/Organization was identified as the leading root cause in 67 of the total 203 processed EMS events.

A management/organization problem was attributed to management methods (directions, monitoring, assessment, accountability, and corrective action), inadequate resource allocation, work organization and planning, supervisory methods, and change management practices.

The reference document Risk and Mitigations for Losing EMS Functions is published biennially and contains analysis and recommendations based on 521 EMS events reported through the ERO EAP between October 2013 and April 2019.

Because the publication/implementation of EOP-004-4 occurred between reference document updates, the NERC EMSWG published NERC Energy Management System Performance Special Assessment (2018–2019) as an interim activity by using 2018–2019 EMS events reported through the ERO EAP.

The ERO Event Analysis Program identified a need to continue the analysis by adding EMS events reported through the ERO EAP in 2020 into the study period for improving resolution on the contribution of EMS outages to the loss of situational awareness and the effect from the EOP-004-4.

Based on the ERO EAP analysis, this document assesses the following factors to evaluate the contribution of EMS outage to loss of situational awareness, risk, and the effect from the EOP-004-4:  Outage Duration Outage duration demonstrates the resilience of an EMS to recover the system or function(s).

Loss or degradation of SCADA means that system operators would not have an indication of the status of devices or of critical substation data points, nor would they be able to open and close breakers, or switches, via remote operator control.
Therefore, the loss of SCADA would likely be the most impactful EMS failure.
This document also examines trends, event root causes, and contributing causes identified through the ERO CCAP for the 2018–2020 period.
The top five contributing causes for the same period will be discussed in detail throughout this document.

Figure 2.7: United States RC EMS Events by Loss of EMS Functions (2018–2020) Based on the analysis of the EMS events reported by RCs, the following recommendations are made to reduce the loss of situational awareness risks due to EMS outage:  Maintaining models up to date The models of the electrical grid are critical for EMS functions.
This is because there is a point of convergence Chapter 2: Analysis and Assessment that may exist at a common hub that becomes a single point of failure.
Therefore, to ensure redundant physical circuit separation and independence of supporting equipment and power, it is recommended that the duration of the service is specified in the contract.
Over these two years, the loss of SE/RTCA was the most prevalent EMS failure in 44% or 78 events of all reported EMS events by TOs/TOPs (see Figure 2.8).
The loss of SE/RTCA events continued to significantly decline from 40 in 2018, to 28 in 2019, and 10 in 2020, similar to the loss of ICCP events.
Of particular note, the loss of SCADA events increased from 21 in 2019 to 27 in 2020.

Chapter 2: Analysis and Assessment Figure 2.10: Median Outage Duration by Loss of EMS Functions—TOs/TOPs (2018–2020) The following observations and recommendations were made during analysis of the EMS events reported by TOs/TOPs:  External Modeling Many entities have expanded their EMS models to monitor the impact of events and outages outside of their footprint.
This has increased potential exposure to bad data points, inaccurate topology modeling, and communication issues that may cause EMS events.

The main advantage of a packet-based network is to transmit data from one node to another node while avoiding a communications system failure caused by the breakdown of a single (or few) intermediate link(s).
Reporting included four complete loss events due to networking packet broadcast storms caused by improper network configurations.

This led to the following recommendations:  Establish standardized settings for network devices  Complete physical separation between SCADA operations networks and business networks, voice over internet protocol (VoIP), and external facing networks is preferred over virtual local area network (VLAN) to avoid network traffic congestion and security issues18  Alarming Alarming has not initiated any EMS events.

It is essential for the entity to not only determine what alarms are needed but also to assess what can cause them to fail or otherwise go unnoticed.19  Power Supply Stable and secure power supplies are critical to control rooms, data centers, and substations.
Sixteen EMS events were due to loss of power supply.

More recommendations can be found in the lessons learned titled Loss of Monitoring or Control Capability due to Power Supply Failure20 and Loss of SCADA Operating and Monitoring Ability.21  Dealing with Abnormal Working Environment In 2020, entities implemented work-from-home policies for non-essential employee.

Balancing Authorities BAs are the responsible entities that integrate resource plans ahead of time, maintain load-interchange-generation balance within a BA area, and support Interconnection frequency in real time.
There were two loss of AGC events reported in 2019 and 2020.
Both loss of AGC events were caused by software bugs introduced during regular AGC software updates.

NERC recognizes AGC as a critical function for a BA and has published a lesson learned titled Loss of Automatic Generation Control during Routine Update 22 to emphasize that a completed software testing process is critical to guarantee that products meet intended requirements.
Two events were caused by firewall hardware failure, and another one was due to an improper firewall configuration.
The loss of SCADA event reported in 2020 was due to a hardware damage caused by a lighting strike.
The loss of RTU event in 2020 was caused by the exhaustion of UPS.
Both were loss of RTU events caused by network device failures.
Analysis of Root Causes and Contributing Causes This section will discuss the event root causes and contributing causes identified through the ERO CCAP for the years 2018 and 2020.
Of the 220 EMS events reported from 2018–2020, 203 EMS events were processed through the ERO CCAP because the processing of 2020 EMS events is ongoing.

causal_questions.question: What EMS function losses formed the main risk mechanism assessed for 2018-2020?
causal_questions.answer: The assessment covered EMS events involving loss of SCADA, ICCP, RTU, AGC, state estimator, or real-time contingency analysis for 30 or more continuous minutes. Across 2018-2020, loss of SE/RTCA was the most prevalent EMS failure, while loss of SCADA became the most prevalent failure in 2020.
causal_questions.notes: Evidence frames the cross-event trigger as reportable EMS function losses and identifies the dominant failure types.

causal_questions.question: What root-cause category most often explained the processed EMS events?
causal_questions.answer: Management/Organization was identified as the leading root-cause category in 67 of 203 processed EMS events. The category included management methods, inadequate resource allocation, work organization and planning, supervisory methods, and change management practices.
causal_questions.notes: Evidence directly states the leading root-cause category, count, and meaning of that category.

causal_questions.question: How can EMS outages propagate into operational situational-awareness risk?
causal_questions.answer: The analysis was intended to improve resolution on how EMS outages contribute to loss of situational awareness. Loss or degradation of SCADA would remove operator indication of device status and critical substation data and prevent remote operation of breakers or switches, making SCADA the likely most impactful EMS failure.
causal_questions.notes: Evidence supports the pathway from EMS outage to loss of monitoring and control capability.

causal_questions.question: What observed reliability impacts did the 2018-2020 EMS function losses have?
causal_questions.answer: From 2018-2020, the loss of EMS functions did not lead to loss of generation, transmission lines, or customer load. Reported EMS events declined from 88 in 2018 to 74 in 2019 and 58 in 2020, while the overall median outage duration stayed near one hour.
causal_questions.notes: Evidence supports a bounded impact answer: no direct BES asset or load loss, with counts and duration trends.

causal_questions.question: What mitigation practices did the assessment recommend for reducing EMS outage and situational-awareness risk?
causal_questions.answer: The assessment recommended maintaining electrical-grid models up to date, specifying service duration in contracts to support redundant physical circuit separation and independent equipment and power, establishing standardized network-device settings, and preferring complete physical separation between SCADA operations networks and business or external-facing networks.
causal_questions.notes: Evidence directly lists recommendations for EMS model quality, circuit redundancy, and network separation.
